title: Minimal Runtime Footprint and Power Budgeting Guide for On‑Prem Appliances
author: Asha Menon
content:
Overview

Purpose: This guide provides a prescriptive cookbook for minimizing the runtime footprint and for creating accurate power budgets for Redwood's on‑prem inference appliances (edge racks and small data‑center footprints). The audience is field engineers, solution architects, hardware partners, and SREs responsible for design, installation, and long‑term ops of private deployments.

Goals:
- Define static and dynamic power envelopes for common appliance classes.
- Provide BIOS/firmware and OS tuning recommendations to reduce idle and tail energy.
- Give runtime (inference) configuration patterns that decrease watt-per-token while preserving SLOs.
- Produce checklists and measurement procedures for pre‑deployment validation and day‑2 ops.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to Redwood Private appliances running our inference runtime (containerized or bare-metal) in customer racks or co‑lo.
- Target models include LLaMA family style models and comparable open checkpoints; for larger proprietary models some recommendations will need recalibration.
- Assumes network power for top-of-rack switch and PDUs are billed separately; this guide focuses on compute node power and cooling.

Key definitions
- Idle power: DC/AC draw with OS booted and no inference workload.
- Baseline runtime power: steady-state power during small steady traffic (1–5 rps) with KV cache cold/warm state defined.
- Burst power: short-lived peaks during heavy parallel inference or model swap.
- Tail energy: incremental power cost to keep memory/GPU warmed between bursts.

High‑level recommendations
1) Aim for predictable baseline: target cluster baseline power per GPU node within +/- 10%. Use conservative rounding up for provisioning.
2) Control idle contributors: NTP, telemetry sampling, and kernel tracing must be throttled in airgapped/private mode.
3) Prefer quantized model artifacts for warm cache steady‑state to reduce both latency and power.
4) Supply a 1.5x burst capacity headroom in the power budget for worst‑case model swap or automated cache rehydration.

Hardware classes and sample power envelopes
| Node class | Typical CPU | GPU Type | Idle (W) | Baseline (W) | Peak burst (W) | Notes |
|-----------|------------:|---------|--------:|-------------:|---------------:|-------|
| Edge‑small | 8‑core Xeon | 1x A4 / <40W | 120W | 300W | 420W | compact chassis, limited cooling 
| Edge‑medium | 16‑core Xeon | 1x A10 / 100W | 160W | 420W | 650W | airflow-optimized chassis 
| DC‑standard | 24+ core | 2x A30 / 250W each | 300W | 900W | 1500W | N+1 PDU recommended 
| Rack‑heavy | Dual CPU | 4x H100 / 350W each | 700W | 2100W | 3500W | enterprise racks, dedicated cooling 

BIOS and firmware tuning checklist
- Disable unused devices (serial ports, on‑board audio) and limit SMBIOS telemetry where allowed.
- Enable power‑budgeting features (cTDP / OEM power cap) when supported.
- Set C‑states aggressive but verify latency impact on cold starts (increase C‑state if acceptable to save idle power).
- Lock CPU frequency scaling governor to "performance" only for nodes that are latency‑sensitive; prefer "ondemand" or "powersave" for lower SLO tiers.

OS and kernel level configuration
- Use latest LTS kernel with perf and cgroupsv2 for power and CPU isolation.
- Configure cpufreq: for inference worker pools use governor="schedutil" or "performance" depending on measured latency impact.
- Reduce sampling frequency for telemetry: default 100 Hz -> 1 Hz on production appliances unless debugging.
- Disable transparent hugepages if it increases memory residency leading to higher baseline power in a given workload.

Inference runtime knobs (APIs / config snippets)
- QuantizationProfile: enable int8/4 artifacts where model verification passes regression tests.
- Batching policy: prefer adaptive continuous batching with a max_latency_ms = 100 for interactive workloads; lower for strict SLOs.
- KV cache TTL: Set short TTL (30s–2m) for highly bursty sets where cold cache energy dominates; longer (5–30m) for sustained traffic to amortize warmup cost.

Example JSON snippet for a conservative runtime profile:
{ "profile_name": "edge-conservative-01", "batching": { "strategy": "adaptive", "max_latency_ms": "100" }, "kv_cache": { "enabled": "true", "ttl_seconds": "120" }, "quantization_profile": "int8-recommended" }

Power measurement procedure (pre‑deployment validation)
1) Environment: connect a calibrated inline power meter to the node PDU branch. Record ambient temperature and rack airflow metrics.
2) Baseline: boot node to OS, wait for 10 minutes of idle steady state. Record Idle power every 10s for 5min.
3) Runtime baseline: start a warm KV cache service and send 1 rps sustained single‑token requests for 10 minutes. Record average.
4) Burst test: replay peak traffic (3–5x expected rps) for 2 minutes. Record peak draw and thermals.
5) Model swap: perform an on‑node model swap (pull artifacts then load) and measure power during the artifact load and first 30s of inference.
6) Report: capture 95th percentile steady and peak values, annotate with firmware, BIOS, and runtime config.

Checklist for field install (P.O. / Rack handoff)
- Confirm PDUs and breakers can sustain 1.5x peak per rack.
- Document per‑unit serial numbers, firmware versions, and applied power caps.
- Validate remote IPMI/iLO access with power cycling scripts in place.
- Deploy telemetry agent with reduced sampling defaults and buffer to local disk when network unavailable.

Day‑2 ops considerations
- Telemetry drift: set alerts for when baseline power deviates >15% from reference for 3 consecutive hours.
- Regression testing: after OS or runtime updates, automatically run a short power regression harness that measures Idle, Baseline, and Swap costs.
- Capacity throttling: attach automated circuit breaker that drops low‑priority queues when sustained cluster power approaches 90% of budget.

Upgrade and rollback implications
- Upgrades can change power characteristics (kernel changes, driver improvements). Require a staged rollout: canary -> 10% -> 50% -> remaining. At each stage run the 20‑minute power regression harness.
- Rollback plan: store previous image artifact and associated BIOS/firmware snapshot where possible. The rollback procedure must include running the validation harness before returning to production traffic.

Operational runbook: quick steps for a rising power alert
1) Alert triggers: baseline drift alert or PDU trip near‑miss.
2) Triage owner: oncall SRE + field operator.
3) Immediate actions: reduce noncritical tenant shares via runtime QoS, reduce telemetry sampling, enable power caps on affected nodes.
4) If power reduction insufficient: gracefully redirect traffic to alternate region/Dedicated pool per routing policy.
5) Post‑incident: capture power profiles, review changes since last good state, create an incident ticket and schedule root cause discussion.

Sizing worksheet (example inputs)
- Expected sustained rps: 300
- Traffic shape: 80% short chats (avg 32 tokens), 20% long completions (avg 512 tokens)
- Candidate node class: DC‑standard (2x A30)
- Measured baseline per node: 900W; measured throughput: 120 rps per node
- Required nodes = ceil(300 / 120) = 3 nodes; baseline budget = 3 * 900W = 2700W; add 1.5x burst factor -> budget = 4050W

Appendices
A. Recommended telemetry keys to collect:
- power.node.total_watts
- gpu[0].power_draw_watts
- cpu.package.power_watts
- kv_cache.hit_ratio
- batching.latency_p50/95/99

B. Sample power check CLI (IPMI + meter)
- ipmitool chassis power status
- ssh root@node "sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime -f | grep power"
- read from inline meter: meterctl --read --channel 1 --duration 30s

C. Ownership and contacts
- Hardware validations and pre‑deploy tests: Field Engineering (field-eng@redwood.com)
- Runtime tuning and profiling: Runtime Team (runtime@redwood.com)
- Escalation for power incidents: Platform SRE (oncall‑platform@redwood.com)
